payload.instruction:
MODE: /transcribe
LANGUAGE: en
INPUT:
When I moved into the flat in September, I thought the hardest part would be carrying everything up two flights of stairs. It turned out to be deciding what counted as essential when the boxes were already full. I had labeled them by room, which seemed sensible until I found the kettle in a box marked “books” and my work notebooks under a bag of winter coats. For the first night, I had a mattress, a lamp, two mugs, and a saucepan. I ate noodles sitting on the floor and felt very pleased with the arrangement, though I had to use my phone as a torch when I went to find the bathroom.

The internet setup took longer than the move. The provider had said the router would arrive on Thursday, so I arranged to work from home that morning. The delivery window changed twice, and then the box turned up while I was in the corner shop buying coffee. My neighbor, Mr. Patel, took it in for me and left a note under my door. The instructions said the wall socket was in the hall, but the cable would not reach the shelf I had picked, so the router spent its first week on a stack of cookbooks. It worked perfectly from there. I still have not moved it.

I bought a desk secondhand from a woman who lived across town. It was heavier than it looked, and the legs came off but the top did not, so my friend Lena and I carried it up the stairs at an angle, stopping on every landing to change hands. We got it into the study, then realized it blocked the cupboard door by about an inch. I could have returned it, but I liked the little scratches on the surface and could open the cupboard if I pulled the desk forward. That is what I do now whenever I need the vacuum cleaner. It has become part of the routine.

The neighbors were friendly from the start, although I had a slightly awkward introduction with the couple next door. I was trying to carry a box of plates and hold the front door open with my foot when they came out with their dog. The dog immediately sniffed the box, and one of the plates slid halfway out. I caught it, but I also said, “That’s not where the dog food is,” which made no sense because I had not bought dog food. They laughed, and we properly introduced ourselves after I put the box down. Now the dog waits by their door whenever it hears me on the stairs, apparently hoping I will have something interesting.

Storage has been a slow puzzle. The flat has a narrow cupboard under the stairs, but the water meter takes up one side and the shelves are too deep for small things. I put cleaning supplies at the back and then forgot they were there, so I bought a second bottle of floor cleaner a week later. I keep the meter cupboard clear now, apart from a folded step stool and a basket of spare light bulbs. The kitchen drawers are better organized. I used small cardboard boxes from the move to separate tea bags, batteries, and all the little clips that come with furniture. They are not attractive, but I can find things without tipping out a whole drawer.

The first work call from the new flat was on a Monday morning, before I had unpacked the curtains. The light came straight through the window and made my face look washed out on camera. I moved the laptop to the other end of the desk, then shifted it again because the router cable was too short. In the end I sat with the window beside me, which was fine once I pulled the blind halfway down. I like having daylight in the room, especially in the afternoon, when the sun reaches the wall above the desk. I keep a small plant there, and it has grown a surprising amount since I moved in.

There was one delivery that I am still embarrassed about, although the driver was kind about it. I had ordered a bookcase and chose a delivery slot for Saturday. The driver rang to say he was downstairs, and I said I would be right there. I went down, opened the front door, and realized the bookcase was much wider than the entrance to the stairwell. We turned it around several times, trying to find an angle, while a neighbor waited behind us with a bag of groceries. Eventually the driver carried it back to the van, and I had to arrange a return. I measured the space properly before ordering a narrower one the next week. That one went up without any trouble.

A few days later, Lena lent me a small screwdriver so I could assemble the bookcase. I expected to have it for an hour, but I put it in a kitchen drawer after finishing and forgot to return it. She asked about it two weeks later, and I found it exactly where I had left it, next to the spare batteries. I took it over that evening, and she teased me about my new storage system. Since then, I have made a point of putting borrowed things by the front door as soon as I bring them inside. It is a simple rule, but it has worked so far.

The flat feels much more settled now, though there are still a couple of unopened boxes in the cupboard. On an ordinary weekend, I make coffee, open the windows for a while, and do one small job rather than trying to finish everything at once. Last Saturday I hung a picture in the hall, then spent the rest of the afternoon reading at the desk while the washing machine ran. In the evening, I went downstairs to take the recycling out and ended up talking with Mr. Patel about the plants on his balcony. Nothing especially dramatic happened, which is probably why I remember the day fondly. It felt like a normal day in a place that had started to feel like home.

MODE: /prompt
LANGUAGE: en
INPUT:
Please review my small personal website and give me practical feedback on its clarity and ease of use. The site is for friends, family, and potential collaborators who want to learn about my work and get in touch. Most visitors will arrive on a phone, though the pages should also work well on a laptop.

The site has three pages. The home page introduces me and links to the other pages. The projects page shows four selected projects, each with a short description and an image. The contact page has my email address and links to my social profiles. I want the site to feel personal and straightforward rather than like a formal portfolio.

Please pay particular attention to accessibility. Note any issues you spot with text contrast, heading structure, image descriptions, keyboard navigation, or whether the links and contact details are easy to identify. If something can’t be assessed from the material provided, please say so rather than guessing.

Please leave the site’s existing colors, personal writing style, and page structure unchanged in your suggestions. I’m looking for observations and small, actionable improvements, not a redesign or new content. Organize your feedback by page, and finish with a short list of the three most important changes to consider.

payload.instruction:
MODE: /polish
LANGUAGE: en
INPUT:
For our neighborhood film night, I started looking for a feature that would work in the small room above the library and still give people something to talk about afterward. We had room for about sixty-five chairs, no stage, and a screen that rolled down in front of a set of old bookshelves. I wanted a film that felt welcoming without being slight, and that could hold the attention of people who rarely went to screenings. The event was planned for a Friday in early October, with doors opening at six and the film beginning at seven.

I made a shortlist of four films and borrowed DVDs from the library, then watched them at home with a notebook beside me. One title had beautiful outdoor scenes but ran nearly two and a half hours, which felt too long for our evening. Another depended on a joke that would have been difficult to explain in the brief introduction. We settled on a quiet, locally made documentary about a family-run ferry service. Its director had filmed the boat over several seasons, and the story offered enough detail to reward close attention without requiring specialist knowledge. I checked the running time twice before confirming the choice: eighty-four minutes.

The screening rights took more discussion than I expected. The library’s usual film license covered its regular program, but the terms were not clear about ticketed community events. I emailed the distributor with the date, room capacity, and proposed ticket price, then waited several days for a reply. The first quote was higher than our entire refreshments budget. I called the distributor’s office and explained that we were a volunteer group rather than a commercial venue. They offered a lower community rate, provided we did not advertise the event as free or make a recording. I shared those terms with the library coordinator before paying the fee.

Captions mattered to several regular visitors, so I checked the disc menu and the distributor’s listing before we announced the film. The DVD included English captions, but the first set I tested was out of sync by a fraction of a second. I contacted the distributor again and learned that the streaming version had a corrected caption file. We were using the DVD, not streaming, so I asked whether we could receive the file separately. They sent a replacement disc the following week. I tested it from beginning to end, including the credits, and the captions stayed in time throughout.

Eight volunteers helped on the night, and I made a simple rota instead of assigning everyone to whatever looked busiest. Mina and Rob set out chairs, while Theo stayed near the entrance to greet people and answer questions about the room. I asked two newer volunteers to handle tickets together, since neither had used our cash box before. We left the first two rows open for people who wanted extra space and marked a clear path to the accessible seats. Just before doors opened, we counted the chairs again and moved four away from the wall so wheelchair users would not have to squeeze past the coat rack.

The projector test happened on Thursday afternoon, when the room was empty and quiet. Our borrowed laptop recognized the projector immediately, but the image was too wide and cut off the subtitles at the bottom. I changed the display setting, then adjusted the projector’s position rather than stretching the picture. A strip of blue painter’s tape on the floor marked the stand’s correct place, and I wrote the laptop’s sound setting on a note beside the remote. We watched the opening five minutes and a scene with particularly dark water, because those were the moments most likely to reveal a focus or brightness problem.

On Friday, the ticket table was ready by half past five. We charged a modest amount at the door and kept a handwritten list for people who had reserved seats by email. A few guests paid with coins, so I brought a small envelope of change from the library office. We had printed forty tickets, but I also brought blank slips in case more people arrived. By six forty-five, the room was nearly full, and Theo stopped taking payments long enough to help an older couple find two seats together. We did not sell the last few tickets, although the room looked busy from the back.

Rain began just as we carried the refreshments upstairs. We had expected cool weather, but not a sudden downpour, and several people arrived with wet coats. The library’s entry mat was already damp, so Mina fetched two extra towels and put a notice near the stairs asking people to leave umbrellas by the door. Tea and apple juice were on the side table, along with biscuits from a bakery on the high street. We kept the hot drinks away from the projector cables and moved the rubbish bin closer to the refreshments when wrappers began collecting on the windowsill.

The audience was quiet during the film, except for a brief laugh at a scene where the ferry’s bell rang while the owner was trying to give an interview. Afterward, several people stayed to talk about how the service had changed over the years. One person had ridden the ferry as a child and recognized the old ticket punch in a close-up. Another asked whether the director had filmed during the winter crossings. I did not know, so I wrote down the question to send to the director rather than guessing. The discussion lasted about twenty minutes, and some guests continued it downstairs as they left.

For another screening, I would like to invite a local filmmaker to speak, if the date and budget allow. We could also try a shorter film followed by a guided discussion, since people seemed comfortable sharing memories once someone asked a specific question. I would reserve a few more seats near the front for people who need an unobstructed view, and I would test the captions on the exact equipment earlier in the week. The library has offered the room again in January, but we have not chosen a film or confirmed a date. For now, I have kept the distributor’s contact details, the volunteer rota, and the projector notes together in one folder.
